detail.abstract: The growing use of AI in adjudication has led to notable failures, such as court orders citing nonexistent cases or misquoting statutes. We analyze how such failures affect public trust in the courts. Drawing on research on judicial legitimacy and algorithmic failure, we develop a framework that distinguishes three types of AI failure: output, process, and perception. We then examine how each affects four dimensions of institutional trust: procedural, epistemic, relational, and moral. A wrong output mostly bears on epistemic trust and may be absorbed, as people blame the ruling or the judge. Conversely, failures revealing that no judge reasoned or took responsibility are different. Such failures may damage the procedural, relational, and moral trust that underlies general confidence in courts, spilling over to other judges and courts. We term such moments "trust shocks" and devise testable propositions about when failures stay local and when they spread. As judges do not fully bear the costs of generating trust shocks, safeguards ought to be institutional. Accordingly, we identify four trustpreserving levers: reason-giving; disclosure of AI use in advance and in the decision record; limits on AI's role that keep a human judge responsible; and testing outputs for stability.

detail.abstract: Macroeconomic news reaches every market in the same second, but prices need seconds to adjust. This paper builds an information diffusion model of that adjustment and uses it to improve a market-making rule. The epidemic part, compartment models and Hawkes processes, measures how fast a release is absorbed. The influence part, a lead-lag network and measures of price discovery, asks which funds and which prediction market move first. The predictive part, cascade models and forecasts of trading activity and volatility, asks which instrument reacts next. The data cover 30 US equity ETFs, Kalshi and Polymarket around every CPI, payrolls and FOMC announcement from January 2025 to October 2026, with the last four months as the hold-out. Eight of fourteen comparisons hold in all 8 hold-out releases. In the first seven seconds after a release a standard Avellaneda-Stoikov quoting rule has a net edge of -2.88 basis points per share on the hold-out, and withdrawing the quotes for those seconds earns more in every hold-out release. Wider quotes around the release raise the net edge from 1.77 to 3.73 basis points per share. Leaving the trade counts of the last seconds out of a forecast of trading activity raises its hold-out error by 305.5%, and a Hawkes forecast of volatility has an error 14.8% higher than a regression on realised volatility. Network cascade models and a lead-lag network do not improve on simple baselines, and the Hawkes branching ratio cannot be estimated from timestamps recorded to the millisecond. In exploratory analyses of the training sample the rule's net edge is lowest between one and two seconds after the release, when the index funds absorb the news, at -3.46 basis points per share. The index funds react a median of 880 ms after 08:30, and resting orders at the best quotes have an edge of -26.59 basis points per share in the first millisecond after that, a span below the resolution of the clock. A rule that withdraws within half a second keeps a share of 0.699 of the gain from withdrawing at once. The order in which the other funds follow can be predicted out of sample, with a mean rank correlation of 0.445, positive in 21 of 21 releases. The comparisons were chosen on the training sample and the small hold-out was used more than once, so each result is labelled as a test or a description.

detail.abstract: This paper develops a risk-shifting explanation for international differences in risk taking based on countries' positions in the global financial network. Theoretically, losses originating in a financially central country spread to foreign households, raising their demand for liquidity and the convenience yield on safe sovereign bonds. The resulting state-contingent funding benefit cushions the originating country's downside, inducing it to take more risk ex ante than a peripheral country. Unlike existing explanations of the exorbitant privilege that emphasize the special role of the U.S., this mechanism operates even when all countries issue bonds with identical safety and liquidity properties. I derive a financial centrality measure that captures how strongly and broadly a country's shock propagates to the rest of the world and show that optimal risk taking increases with centrality. Empirically, financial centrality is positively associated with external risky-asset shares, firm operating risk (ROA volatility), and risky investment (R&D intensity).

detail.abstract:
A new specter is haunting job seekers in the post-COVID-19 economy: "ghost jobs," which are job listings by real companies advertising positions that do not actually exist or for which there is no present intention to hire. Ghost jobs do not simply waste the time and money of job applicants. They also reflect a new evolution in the harvesting and misuse of sensitive personal data, which inflicts privacy wounds on individuals while breaching the modern social contract on which the digital economy runs. Ghost jobs also distort the economic data that inform critical nationwide policy decisions, such as the setting of federal interest rates. Nonetheless, the prevailing view is that ghost jobs, while regrettable, do not run afoul of any U.S. law. 

This Piece challenges that notion, arguing that ghost jobs violate the consumer protection mandates of the Federal Trade Commission Act. The FTC should use its enforcement authority over unfair and deceptive consumer practices to exorcise ghost jobs from the online hiring landscape. This Piece offers a roadmap for doing so.

detail.abstract: Cybersecurity is typically viewed as a defensive investment whose economic value lies in the losses it prevents. We argue that it can also be productive. By reducing disruptions and uncertainty and strengthening trust in digital systems, cybersecurity can increase the returns to digital adoption and investment. We test this hypothesis by asking whether improvements in national cybersecurity preparedness disproportionately benefit sectors that depend more heavily on digital inputs. Exploiting variation in digital dependence across sectors and changes in preparedness within countries, we find that a one-standard-deviation improvement in preparedness is associated with approximately 0.6 percentage points faster annual growth in a sector with one-standard-deviation greater digital exposure. These findings recast cybersecurity not merely as protection against economic losses, but as a productive complement to digitalization. (H56, L86, O11, O14, O33).

detail.abstract: While many people have a concrete idea of what "cyberwar" or "cyberwarfare" is, they haven't for the term "cyber peace." Although "cyber peace" is now mentioned more frequently, the term is rarely defined in concrete terms. Used interchangeably as an end state, a governance objective and a bundle of practices, the term labels almost any cooperative security activity and therefore discriminates almost nothing. This article argues that the confusion is ontological rather than terminological and resolves it with a condition-capacity-process model: recurrent practices build institutional capacity when they are trusted, resourced and institutionalised; capacity lowers the probability that harm becomes severe or systemic; and crises supply, or withhold, the learning that revises both. The outcome of this process model can be described as a two-dimensional Cyber Peace Space that distinguishes among brittle calm, cyber disorder, robust cyber peace, and contested resilience. It is demonstrated that the model description of cyber peace presented here serves as the foundation for new tools, such as a Peace-by-Design framework and requirements for response conformity, to ensure cyber peace. It is discussed how further developments can serve as the foundation for a discipline of cyber peace.

detail.abstract: Voice input and generative AI are changing how employees compose workplace feedback, yet little is known about their individual and combined effects on feedback contribution. Drawing on cognitive load, media naturalness, and social presence theories, we argue that voice input lowers the cost of generating ideas and elicits richer content, whereas AI refinement lowers the cost of organizing and polishing it, though repeated use may foster reliance that erodes engagement. We test this argument in an eight-week, twophase randomized field experiment on FDBCK, a commercial real-time peer-feedback application deployed in the research and development division of a multinational consumer packaged goods company. In Phase 1, we randomly assigned 300 employees to a 2 × 2 design crossing input format (voice vs. text) with AI assistance (no AI vs. basic AI refinement). Voice input primarily raises engagement, as employees give feedback more often and write longer, more positive messages. Basic AI refinement primarily renders feedback more specific, actionable, and helpful to recipients, with a smaller effect on engagement. When combined with voice input, the AI has richer content to refine, and its specificity gain is roughly three times that under typing. Its engagement and helpfulness gains decay over time, however. In Phase 2, an enhanced AI function structures the feedback task into components, focusing contributors' effort while preserving their input, and further improves effectiveness without reducing engagement.

detail.abstract:
Small and medium-sized businesses (SMBs) — firms with fewer than 500 employees — are the backbone of U.S. employment, accounting for almost half of private sector jobs and the lion’s share of new openings. Despite their outsized role in employment growth, SMBs often receive less attention in workforce development research and policy discussions than their larger enterprise counterparts. Therefore, understanding how SMBs approach talent acquisition and identifying scalable strategies to support more inclusive hiring practices, such as skills-based hiring, is critical to advancing workforce equity at scale.

Results from qualitative interviews and a survey fielded to SMB owners and hiring managers suggest that SMBs hire fast but not always well. They see fewer applicants per role and assign great weight to intuitive evaluation and cultural fit. Because their practices feel sufficient in the moment, SMBs perceive little need to change them, but a 21% six-month departure rate for new hires suggests that their lean pipelines and intuitive approach come at a cost. Skills-based hiring adoption among SMBs may best be described as widespread in name and shallow in practice. Reported adoption is near-universal (97%), and hiring managers express high enthusiasm. But two of the reforms that skills-based hiring advocates treat as prerequisites —removing unnecessary degree requirements and explicitly using skills to connect candidates to roles — are poorly represented in actual behavior. This points to a pattern of layering skills language onto an existing intuition-driven process rather than replacing credential screening with a structured, systematic practice. The result is skills-aware hiring rather than skills-first hiring — a distinction that matters because the outcomes that skills-based hiring promises (broader talent pools, reduced credential bias, and better match quality) depend on the underlying reforms, not just the attitude toward them.

The barrier to more genuine embrace of skills-based hiring is not attitude or technology but information infrastructure. SMB hiring managers are genuinely receptive to independently verified evidence that a candidate can do the job. They are more receptive to it, in fact, than to any other signal, including credentials. Given reliable skills evidence, they will use it over degree requirements. But two capabilities remain out of reach for most: defining roles by the skills that matter and assessing those skills reliably. This gap holds across all SMBs. Any scalable intervention must treat it as a baseline problem to solve. At the same time, and despite sharing a common foundational challenge, SMBs are not a monolith. Structural characteristics — firm size, industry, organizational type — can explain some of the variations in SMB hiring activity and practice, but mindset offers a more analytically useful lens. Three distinct orientations emerge from the data, each with a different relationship to skills- based hiring:

Network hirers source primarily through referrals and lean on relational, trust-based hiring logic; their entry point for intervention is expanding candidate
pipelines while formalizing the durable-skills evaluation they already do intuitively.

Deficit-driven hirers must grapple with overcoming constraints of one kind or another in the roles they have to offer. They face the most acute hiring failures
— the slowest time-to-hire and turnover nearly three times that of growth hirers— and are motivated by overcoming challenges; they need low-cost, easily
integrated tools and support in turning skills they can already identify into effective screening and promotion.

Growth hirers are the most process-oriented and technology-engaged segment, already investing in skills-based infrastructure; their challenge is refinement, not adoption, as well as a need for evidence that what they are doing is working.

The shared skills-definition-and-assessment gap requires a common baseline solution, but closing it effectively will mean tailoring outreach, tooling, and messaging to each mindset’s distinct motivations and constraints. Because SMBs collectively account for such a large share of U.S. hiring activity, even modest improvements in how they define and assess skills could meaningfully expand opportunity for workers historically screened out by credential requirements.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is now widely piloted in manufacturing, yet many pilots do not become dependable production systems. This paper argues that the main obstacle is not algorithmic capability but the absence of a decision-centred design discipline that links data, models, people and governance. Drawing on the author's book AI-Driven Production Management (2026), it proposes a framework in which every AI application starts from a named operational decision, its owner and a measured baseline, and is bounded by explicit authority limits, human override and monitoring. The framework is applied across four core domains: quality control, production scheduling, supply-chain management and predictive maintenance. It is extended to digital twins, agentic AI and large language models. A reproducible synthetic case study on component-readiness prediction for a hypothetical UK hydraulic-equipment manufacturer illustrates the evaluation discipline. A gradient boosting classifier reached a ROC-AUC of 0.669 against 0.587 for a transparent rule, while the rule kept higher recall (0.768 against 0.652). The paper also sets out stage gates with kill criteria, an NPV sensitivity showing that a 40% shortfall in benefit realisation can turn a positive case negative, and the UK and EU regulatory position as of October 2026. Implications for practice and research are discussed.

detail.abstract: This paper provides the first independent event-study analysis of the three SEBI-documented YouTube-based pump-and-dump cases in Indian equities, namely the manipulations of Sadhna Broadcast Limited, Sharpline Broadcast Limited, and Atlantaa Limited documented in SEBI orders of 2 March 2023 and 30 April 2025. Using daily price and volume data from BSE India and the BSE SmallCap Index as the market benchmark, abnormal returns and standardised abnormal volume are computed around the documented YouTube upload dates following the market-model framework of MacKinlay (1997). For Sadhna Broadcast, the cumulative abnormal return over the eleven trading days from the first video upload is +37.9 per cent (t = 2.97, p < 0.01); for Atlantaa Limited, the analogous figure is +32.4 per cent (t = 2.65, p < 0.01), followed by a significant reversal of -27.0 per cent in the [+11, +20] window. Abnormal trading volume is highly significant in every post-event window for all three cases. Two of the three cases (Atlantaa, -27.0 per cent; Sharpline, -78.2 per cent) show statistically significant post-event price reversals, the classic pump-and-dump signature. The Atlantaa reversal is, to the author's knowledge, among the largest documented on a regulator-verified social-media manipulation in the published or working-paper literature. The comparable magnitude of effects on a small-cap and a micro-cap stock complicates a simple size-based account of vulnerability to YouTube-based manipulation.

detail.abstract:
This paper develops an exponentially weighted endpoint coordinate for a time series and identifies Wilder’s Relative Strength Index (RSI) as an affine representation of that coordinate. With a recursive mean M_t, signed increment smoother S_t, and absolute-increment smoother A_t, all using gain α, the matched finite-path identity is

X_t − M_t = ((1 − α)/α) S_t, with |S_t| ≤ A_t.

For Wilder gain α = 1/n, the normalized endpoint displacement is therefore bounded by n − 1. Writing F_t = S_t/A_t gives the exact chain

RSI_t/100 = (1 + F_t)/2, and L_t = logit(RSI_t/100) = 2 atanh(F_t).

These identities are distribution-free. The exponential kernel has exact squared energy 1/(2n − 1) and exact Kish effective length 2n − 1. Under stationary centered i.i.d. increments with variance σ² < ∞ and m₁ = E|ε| > 0, the full log-odds coordinate satisfies

sqrt(2n − 1) · m₁/(2σ) · L_t^(n) ⇒ N(0,1).

Equivalently, sqrt(n) · L_t^(n)/C_F ⇒ N(0,1), where C_F = 2σ/m₁. Under a finite third absolute moment, an exact event reduction yields a Berry–Esseen bound of order n^(−1/2) for the full nonlinear log ratio. Under stronger symmetry and light-tail assumptions, its variance admits the finite-horizon expansion

Var(L_n) = v₁α + v₂α² + v₃α³ + v₄α⁴ + O(α⁵), with α = 1/n,

where v₁, …, v₄ are explicit functions of normalized absolute moments. Series inversion yields a law-specific variance-normalizing length

g_F*(n) = C_F²/Var(L_n) = n − K_F + A_F/n + B_F/n² + O(n^(−3)).

For Laplace increments this gives g_L*(n) = n − 4/3 + 5/(18n) + 5/(27n²) + O(n^(−3)); Gaussian increments produce different, π-dependent coefficients. A companion Lean 4 development checks the exact pathwise identities, the Wilder recursion bridge, kernel energy, local log-odds transfer, and a finite-variance limit theorem for normalized finite linear rows. The stationary nonlinear limit, Berry–Esseen bound, and fourth-order analytic remainder are proved by conventional arguments; the coefficient algebra is independently reproduced by a pinned SymPy calculation. No trading rule or predictive claim is made.

detail.abstract: Theories of affect-cued recall suggest that negative emotional shocks should worsen economic sentiment, with stronger shocks generating more negative responses. Our findings challenge this prediction, using foreign earthquakes as plausibly exogenous shocks to US consumer sentiment that are unrelated to domestic economic fundamentals. We document a nonlinear response: earthquakes of magnitude 6.5-7.49 reduce sentiment by 2.31 index points, whereas earthquakes of magnitude 7.5 or greater increase it by 5.73 points. To explain this reversal, we develop a model featuring two competing mechanisms: emotional responses and the displacement of economic information. We document three empirical findings: the magnitude-dependent reversal in sentiment, a 4.80-percentage-point decline in households' reported economic-news recall following major earthquakes, and a corresponding reduction in economic-news airtime on US cable television. Together, these findings are consistent with information displacement outweighing adverse emotional effects when the displaced economic information is predominantly unfavorable. For policymakers, the results suggest that changes in the information environment may reverse the sentiment response from negative to positive, even without changes in economic fundamentals.

detail.abstract: The present study compares mastery of phronesis (i.e., practical wisdom) between business school students and students in other schools at a joint-venture university in China. We inquired whether business students’ practical wisdom was more evident or less evident compared with the non-business students. Our question was motivated by the existing research in the business ethics literature that does not provide a ‘happy reading’ about business students, whose qualities are often associated with dishonesty, greed, corruption, and selfishness, more so than those of non-business students. We utilised the Short Phronesis Measure (SPM), which was recently developed and validated; it assesses moral functioning holistically, different from most conventional measures that focus only on individual traits or virtue/vice constructs. We collected data from 653 participants (business students, n=289; non-business students, n=364). Our Bayesian analysis of the data showed that business students’ phronesis mastery was not significantly different from that of non-business students in all domains. The finding suggests that business students are not inferior in phronetic moral functioning in general. This serves as an important reminder for business school educators that business students have the same potential as other students to achieve moral excellence.

detail.abstract: Digital platforms are changing how firms design, coordinate, and govern operations by integrating artificial intelligence, blockchain, digital sensing and digital twins, data infrastructure, and additive manufacturing. This paper develops a selective research agenda for production and operations management by distinguishing enabling technologies from the platforms, workflows, and business models through which they are deployed. We organize the agenda around a common sequence linking technological capability, operational manifestation, mechanism, outcomes, and boundary conditions. The relevant mechanisms include prediction, information visibility, verification, orchestration, monitoring, human override, and decision rights. We articulate how these mechanisms may create operational value through improvements in productivity, quality, responsiveness, resilience, compliance, and customer experience, enabling firms to capture financial value through revenue growth, cost reduction, risk avoidance, and improved asset utilization. We first identify enduring operations management themes that emerging technologies may reshape. We then develop five forward-looking paths involving artificial intelligence-enabled business-tobusiness platforms, physical-digital integration, agentic service workflows, data and artificial intelligence governance, and platform-enabled resilience under geopolitical disruption. Finally, we discuss theoretical and methodological approaches that can support cumulative research.

detail.abstract: Many young shoppers care about the environment, but caring and paying a higher price are different things. This paper examines that distinction using Choice Par Charcha, a 2026 survey by the United Nations Development Programme and Youth Ki Awaaz with 10,149 valid responses from across India. In its weighted findings, 48% said they think "a lot" about how a purchase affects others, and 51% said environmental impact had crossed their mind during a recent purchase. This paper therefore uses the published results to clarify the evidence, checks a discrepancy in one barrier chart, and sets out a purchase experiment for the questions that remain. detail.abstract: This paper examines whether a tax on a formalized digital financial channel can reverse the financial inclusion gains the channel was designed to deliver, using Ghana's Electronic Transfer Levy as a natural experiment. The levy was introduced at 1.5 per cent on digital transfers in May 2022, reduced to 1 per cent in January 2023, and repealed in March 2025, generating staggered rate variation that supports a dose-response identification strategy. Using quarterly Bank of Ghana administrative data covering 2017-2023, I estimate that the 1.5 per cent rate is associated with a 21 per cent decline in transaction values; the 1 per cent rate produces no statistically detectable effect. The attenuation coincides with the rate cut despite a worsening macroeconomic crisis, identifying the levy's effect through the temporal asymmetry between the two. A within-mobile-money difference-indifferences using the statutorily exempt cash-out channel as control and a cross-channel comparison of annual growth rates corroborate the dose-response result. Disaggregated evidence, cashout transactions rising 44 per cent, person-to-business transactions falling 63 per cent, is consistent with substitution toward cash and informal channels. The findings carry direct implications for at least twelve African governments that have implemented or are actively considering similar levies.

detail.abstract: AI-driven recommendation systems are increasingly used in transportation to suggest routes, modes, and multimodal journeys, yet their opacity can undermine user trust and adoption. This study developed and evaluated a framework for generating human-understandable justifications for transportation recommendations. The framework combined model-agnostic feature attribution with a natural language generation module to produce contrastive and counterfactual explanations tailored to user context. We conducted a mixed-methods user study with 180 participants across route-choice and multimodal journey scenarios, comparing feature-based, contrastive, counterfactual, and hybrid explanation styles against a noexplanation baseline. Results showed that explanations significantly improved user comprehension, trust, and satisfaction. Counterfactual explanations were most effective for route-choice decisions, increasing comprehension by 32% and trust by 24% relative to the baseline, while feature-based explanations were more effective for multimodal trade-offs involving cost and environmental impact. Hybrid explanations achieved the highest overall satisfaction and were rated most useful for adoption decisions. Mediation analysis indicated that trust and comprehension jointly predicted participants' intention to follow recommendations. The study contributes a validated explanation framework and design principles for transparent, trustworthy transportation recommendation systems.

detail.abstract: This study examines whether graded sports trading cards can serve as an uncorrelated alternative store of value alongside gold and digital assets. Using completed sales recorded in the Professional Sports Authenticator (PSA) Auction Prices Realized database, I build an equalweighted, buy-and-hold portfolio of seven iconic cards from baseball, basketball, football, and hockey that span seven decades. The portfolio is compared with Bitcoin, an equal-weighted basket of five cryptocurrencies, gold futures, and the S&P 500 from November 2023 to November 13, 2026. Over the period months, the card portfolio returned 192.02% before costs (42.93% compound annual growth) with annualized volatility of 31.12%, a maximum drawdown of-30.22%, and a Sortino ratio of 2.83. Its monthly returns were essentially uncorrelated with the S&P 500 (r =-.068), Bitcoin (r =-.077), the cryptocurrency basket (r =-.079), and gold (r =-.028). Even so, Memmel-adjusted Jobson-Korkie tests show that the Sharpe ratio advantage over each benchmark is not statistically significant at this horizon. Selling costs also matter; a 13% marketplace fee and a 20% auction consignment fee lower annualized returns to 36.45% and 32.69%. The cards outperformed on a gross and a net basis in this cycle and showed no detectable correlation with financial markets, but illiquidity, custody requirements, and transaction costs set them apart from liquid securities.

detail.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has the potential to fundamentally change how evidence is gathered, understood and used in policymaking. The pace of change is likely faster than governments and traditional governance processes can manage. Yet enthusiasm for AI is considerable, with governments across the world seeking to embrace its power to improve public services, drive efficiency and make better decisions for the public good. This rapid scoping review of the literature attempts to take stock of these changes and explore if and how AI is being integrated into evidencebased practices and what effect this may have on the policy process. Using scoping review methods and drawing from 22 sources, the literature describes a range of advantages and potential benefits of AI in Evidence Informed Policy Making. In particular, AI can assist in quickly making sense of large volumes of data, support evidence synthesis and streamline bureaucratic processes. These potential benefits, however, are moderated by a series of serious concerns and limitations, many of which impact the foundations on which evidence is built, understood and applied to policy problems. Critical perspectives highlight both ethical and epistemic concerns. Alongside this, themes emerging from analysis highlighted how the design of AI tools intersect with the orientations and environments of policy makers, producing a confluence of capabilities, opportunities and motivations that likely drive ongoing use. The paper concludes with a discussion of future directions for the field of AI-mediated Evidence Informed Policy Making and offers an agenda for enquiries into it.

detail.abstract: We analyze the impact of the political business cycle (PBC), the tendency for governments to stimulate the economy immediately prior to elections to increase the likelihood of remaining in office, on firm performance in 24 Sub-Saharan African countries. We formalize our intuition with a conceptual framework and test our hypotheses using panel data from the World Bank Enterprise Surveys (WBES). We show that firms in countries outside of the two CFA monetary unions benefit from the PBC during election years, while within the CFA, there is little impact on firms on average. These findings are consistent with the monetary and fiscal constraints associated with CFA membership dampening the effects of the PBC on firms. We also find important differences across firm types: exporting firms in CFA countries benefit relative to non-exporting firms, multi-establishment firms outside the CFA benefit disproportionately, and firms reporting that informal payments to public officials are common among similar establishments perform relatively worse during election years. Finally, our findings are broadly robust to alternative specifications and wild cluster bootstrap inference.

detail.abstract: Sixth-generation (6G) networks are expected to support UAV missions whose communication requirements are defined not by raw throughput alone but by the meaning and timeliness of the information exchanged. This 2023 research topic investigates a shift from spectrum-centric to semantics-centric slice differentiation for UAV missions in 6G. Conventional slicing differentiates services by bandwidth, latency, and reliability, but UAV missions such as surveillance, search-and-rescue, and payload delivery often require only task-relevant semantic features to be delivered reliably and on time, while tolerating substantial reduction in bit volume. The research topic proposes a framework in which mission tasks are characterized by their task-relevant meaning, and this meaning is mapped onto differentiated slice profiles that govern semantic extraction, transmission, and reconstruction across the 6G infrastructure. Key research questions include how to formalize task-relevant meaning for representative UAV missions, how to translate semantic requirements into slice-level resource and QoS parameters, and how to enforce slice isolation when slices differ in semantic rather than spectral terms. The topic also examines the interplay between semantic slicing and legacy spectrum-based slicing, with attention to coexistence, backward compatibility, and orchestration overhead. The expected outcome is a conceptual architecture and evaluation methodology for semanticsaware 6G slice differentiation, assessed against spectrum-centric baselines in terms of resource efficiency, mission success, and robustness to channel variability. The topic is defined within the state of research available in 2023 and does not depend on later developments.

detail.abstract: Higher education has a human capital problem that conventional human resource management struggles to see. In recent United States survey data, one in four college and university staff members say they are likely to look for another job within a year, 72 percent of supervisors report working beyond full-time hours, and the median provost has been in post for two years. Most institutional HR functions, meanwhile, still report vacancies filled rather than capability built. This paper develops the HELIX framework, a dual-strand architecture for academic human capital that treats every HR practice as a coupled pair: what the individual scholar experiences, and what the institution is actually able to deliver. HELIX organises practice into five strands: Hiring intelligence, Experience and equity, Learning and leadership, Insight and analytics, and eXchange with the wider economy. Alongside the strands sits a five-layer Academic Talent Intelligence Stack, which moves an institution from record keeping to predictive and then agentic people operations, with an explicit ethical gate at each step. The paper offers three instruments that an HR office can use directly. The first is the Academic Human Capital Index (AHCI), a 0 to 100 composite of twenty indicators with a coupling coefficient, so that an institution cannot score well by excelling on one strand while neglecting another. The second is a five-level maturity rubric with observable descriptors for each strand. The third is a twenty-five item diagnostic questionnaire with anchored response scales. We demonstrate the framework on four simulated institutional archetypes and set out a thirty-six month implementation roadmap with decision gates. The contribution is prescriptive rather than empirical. HELIX is offered as a testable design, and the paper closes with the validation agenda it now needs.

detail.abstract: Digital identity policy treats people and businesses as two separate subjects, each with its own registries, credentials and compliance checks. This paper argues that the split is the wrong starting point, and that AI agents make it urgent to fix. It proposes one model. The person is the originating identity. Over a lifetime, a person holds roles, each granted by someone with the authority to grant it: the law, an employer, a government program, or another person through a power of attorney. The grantor can scope, change or revoke the role, and any role can be bound to an agent. The paper sets out the model, tests it against Canadian law, locates it among related work in Europe, the United Kingdom and the standards community, and recommends how Canada’s digital credentials pilot could use it.

detail.abstract: This generic qualitative inquiry explored how LGBTQ+ business leaders in the United States understood and used emotional intelligence while navigating identity-related workplace demands during organizational change. Goleman’s four-domain emotional intelligence model served as a sensitizing framework. Semistructured Zoom interviews were analyzed using Braun and Clarke’s reflexive thematic analysis. detail.abstract: Financial crises in emerging market economies (EMEs) rarely remain confined to their country of origin. Episodes ranging from the 1997 Asian crisis to the 2013 taper tantrum and the 2020 pandemic sell-off show that distress travels through trade, banking, portfolio, and sentiment channels. This paper develops an integrated framework that combines network analysis and machine learning (ML) to measure, explain, and predict contagion across twenty emerging economies. The empirical design is grounded in the first-, second-, and third-generation currency crisis models, global games, herding and information cascades, the financial accelerator, bank-run and funding-liquidity theory, and network cascade models, and the paper derives testable hypotheses from each. First, we build timevarying financial networks using generalized forecast error variance decompositions from vector autoregressions, sparse partial-correlation graphs estimated by the graphical lasso, and a multilayer representation combining market, trade, and banking exposures. Second, wederive network centrality measures and a spectral amplification index and show theoretically that systemic vulnerability is governed by the spectral radius of the exposure matrix. Third, we feed network-based features together with macro-financial fundamentals into regularized logistic regression, random forests, gradient boosting, long short-term memory (LSTM) networks, and graph convolutional networks (GCN) to predict the probability that a country enters a crisis within the next one to six months. We evaluate performance outof-sample with time-series cross-validation, receiver operating characteristic analysis, and Diebold–Mariano tests, and interpret models with Shapley values. The framework yields the architecture of the empirical design, the estimators, the loss functions and the evaluation protocol; the numerical results presented are illustrative of the expected layout and should be substituted with replication output. The proposed approach shows how adding network topology to fundamentals can improve early warning performance, and it offers policymakers a transparent method for monitoring systemic importance and cross-border vulnerability. detail.abstract:
In the wars of choice of recent decades, military ethics was often promoted on the grounds
that ethical conduct enhances operational effectiveness. This paper explains how that
functional argument underlies Just War Theory and professional military ethics education,
both of which frequently emphasize the usefulness of ethical behaviour—especially in
efforts to win hearts and minds both locally and globally. However, this rationale fails when
unethical conduct appears more effective, as may be the case in the ‘wars of necessity’ that
many political and military leaders now foresee. In such conflicts, ethical constraints will be
perceived as hindrances to success. This paper concludes that the relationship between
ethics and effectiveness is, at best, indirect. Consequently, relying on effectiveness to justify
ethics education for military personnel is not only unconvincing but also morally
unsatisfactory.
